title: I Haven't Slept Well in 17 Years
author: Anthony B. Bradley
summary: Anthony Bradley uses his own 17-year struggle with sleep disruption as the entry point for a social-science review of sleep disturbances in middle-aged men. Drawing on a 9-year longitudinal study of 1,721 workers, he examines how job strain—high demands combined with low control—predicts persistent sleep problems over years, not just weeks. Bradley traces his own case to 2009, when he entered a high-demand, low-control professional environment as the first Black professor at a denominational seminary, and the chronic sleep disruption that followed never fully resolved. He argues this pattern is widespread among middle-aged men yet no institution is positioned to address it, and that younger men should treat this data as a warning.
points: Job strain—high demands combined with low control over one's situation—predicts persistent, multi-year sleep disturbances, not just short-term disruption.
A 9-year longitudinal study of 1,721 workers (average age 51) confirmed that every formulation of job strain tested pointed to the same conclusion: sleep suffers for years.
Bradley's own case began in 2009 in a high-demand, low-control academic environment; the chronic sleep disruption lasted 17 years and counting.
This pattern is a documented problem for middle-aged men specifically, yet no institution—medical, religious, or professional—seems positioned to address it.
For younger men, the data serves as a warning: the conditions that produce chronic sleep disruption are common, and the consequences compound over time.
quotes: This is particularly a problem for middle-aged men, yet no institution seems positioned to address it.

The findings were clear. High job strain at baseline predicted a significant increase in sleep disturbances over time. Every formulation of job strain the researchers tested pointed to the same conclusion.
If your job puts heavy demands on you and gives you little say in how things get done, your sleep is going to suffer. Not just for a few weeks, but for years.
I found myself working ridiculously long hours and sleeping around 4 hours per night. I didn’t have a problem falling asleep (that’s depression). I struggled to stay asleep (that’s anxiety).
Job strain is characterized as a combination of high job demands and low job control.
All of this tells us something sad and profound about the current state of American life.
